title: High income improves evaluation of life but not emotional well-being
book_use: Chapter 1: establishes distinction between life evaluation and emotional well-being and the influential approximately $75,000 plateau result in 2008–2009 U.S. data.

title: Experienced well-being rises with income, even above $75,000 per year
book_use: Chapter 1: experience-sampling result based on more than 1.7 million reports from 33,391 employed U.S. adults; no general plateau at the earlier threshold.

author_or_institution: Matthew A. Killingsworth; Daniel Kahneman; Barbara Mellers
title: Income and emotional well-being: A conflict resolved
book_use: Chapter 1: reconciles earlier findings; flattening among least-happy participants while well-being continues rising for happier groups. Preserve observational and measurement caveats.

author_or_institution: Philip Brickman; Dan Coates; Ronnie Janoff-Bulman
title: Lottery winners and accident victims: Is happiness relative?
book_use: Chapter 2: canonical early adaptation study. Winners not significantly happier than controls and reported less pleasure from ordinary events; accident victims reported lower present happiness than controls, so adaptation is real but partial.

author_or_institution: Ed Diener; Richard E. Lucas; Christine Napa Scollon
title: Beyond the Hedonic Treadmill: Revising the Adaptation Theory of Well-Being
book_use: Chapter 2: five revisions to set-point theory — non-neutral set points, individual differences, multiple components, changeable set points, and differential adaptation.

title: Adaptation and the Set-Point Model of Subjective Well-Being: Does Happiness Change After Major Life Events?
book_use: Chapter 2: panel-data evidence that divorce, widowhood, unemployment, and disability are associated with lasting changes in well-being; adaptation is not inevitable and varies by person.

author_or_institution: Maike Luhmann; Wilhelm Hofmann; Michael Eid; Richard E. Lucas
title: Subjective Well-Being and Adaptation to Life Events: A Meta-Analysis
book_use: Chapter 2: integration of 188 publications on reaction and adaptation to family and work events; marriage adapted within about two years while negative events adapted more slowly and less completely, and cognitive well-being responded differently from affective well-being.

author_or_institution: Rafael Di Tella; John Haisken-De New; Robert MacCulloch
title: Happiness Adaptation to Income and to Status in an Individual Panel
book_use: Chapter 2: German Socio-Economic Panel, 1984–2000; most of income's effect on life satisfaction dissipated within about four years while status effects persisted — the income/status asymmetry.

author_or_institution: Andrew E. Clark; Conchita D'Ambrosio; Simone Ghislandi
title: Adaptation to Poverty in Long-Run Panel Data
book_use: Chapter 2: falling into poverty produced large and persistent declines in life satisfaction with little evidence of adaptation — used to keep the book from moralizing scarcity.

title: The Challenge of Staying Happier: Testing the Hedonic Adaptation Prevention Model
book_use: Chapter 2: hedonic adaptation prevention — variety and continued appreciation slow the decay of well-being gains from positive life changes.

title: Drugs, Brains, and Behavior: The Science of Addiction
book_use: Chapter 5: reward circuitry, tolerance, compulsive drug use, and limits of treating ordinary preference as addiction by analogy.

title: American Time Use Survey
book_use: Chapter 8: empirical baseline for paid work, sleep, leisure, caregiving, and other uses of finite daily time.

title: Bringing Dark Patterns to Light
book_use: Chapter 9 and platform-design material: documented interface practices that can steer or manipulate user behavior; use to distinguish deliberate design from vague claims about addictive technology.

title: Problems of Monetary Management: The U.K. Experience
book_use: Chapter 11: historical source behind Goodhart's law; verify exact language and separate original claim from later formulations about metrics becoming targets.

author_or_institution: Gilles Duranton and Matthew A. Turner
title: The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion: Evidence from US Cities
book_use: Chapter 13: induced-demand evidence showing vehicle kilometers traveled increasing roughly proportionally with lane kilometers in U.S. interstate highways; examine limitations and policy context.

title: Engineering Statistics Handbook
book_use: Chapter 14: reliability, optimization, process capability, and diminishing-return examples; use specific sections only after verifying the exact engineering claim.
